reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Ashcraft Pediatric Surgery
clinicalPearls: A spectrum of congenital defects in which the rectum and anus fail to develop normally, ranging from a low membranous covering to a high rectum ending in a fistula to the urinary tract or vagina
Usually detected on the routine newborn examination when no normal anal opening is found, or when the neonate fails to pass meconium and develops abdominal distension
Classified broadly as low (perineal) or high (supralevator) lesions, which guides whether a primary perineal repair or an initial diverting colostomy is required
Meconium seen at the perineum, in the urine, or from the vagina points to an associated fistula and helps localise the level of the malformation
Frequently forms part of the VACTERL association, so vertebral, cardiac, tracheo-oesophageal, renal, and limb anomalies should be actively sought
Reconstruction is typically by posterior sagittal anorectoplasty, performed primarily in low lesions or in stages after a protective colostomy in high lesions
Long-term follow-up focuses on continence and constipation, which correlate with the height of the lesion and the integrity of the sacrum and sphincter complex
reference.pathophysiology: Anorectal malformation arises from disordered development of the hindgut and cloaca during early gestation, when the urorectal septum normally partitions the cloaca into an anterior urogenital sinus and a posterior anorectal canal, and the anal membrane subsequently perforates. Failure or incomplete progression of this process leaves the rectum terminating blindly or connecting abnormally to the urinary tract, vagina, or perineum through a fistula. The level at which the bowel ends relative to the levator ani (puborectalis) sling determines whether the lesion is low or high and how well-developed the striated sphincter musculature and sacrum are, which in turn predicts continence.
additionalDifferentials: Meconium plug syndrome or small left colon
Hirschsprung disease presenting with distal obstruction
Colonic or rectal atresia with a patent anus
additionalInvestigations: Careful perineal inspection for an anal opening, fistula, and the perineal 'bucket-handle' or flat-bottom appearance
Cross-table lateral prone (invertogram-type) radiograph to estimate the level of the distal rectal gas
Urinalysis and inspection for meconium in urine to detect a rectourinary fistula
Echocardiography, renal and spinal ultrasound, and spinal imaging to screen for VACTERL and tethered cord
Distal colostogram before definitive repair to define the fistula and rectal anatomy
Sacral radiograph to assess the sacral ratio as a prognostic marker for continence
redFlags: Progressive abdominal distension and bilious vomiting from unrelieved distal obstruction
Absent anus with no fistula, indicating a high lesion that needs urgent surgical decompression
Meconium in the urine signalling a rectourinary fistula and risk of urosepsis
Associated major cardiac or renal anomalies compromising the neonate
Features of a cloacal malformation with a single perineal opening requiring specialist assessment
reference.prognosis: Low lesions with a well-formed sacrum and sphincter complex generally achieve good continence after repair, whereas high or cloacal lesions and sacral hypoplasia carry higher rates of faecal incontinence and constipation. Structured bowel management and long-term multidisciplinary follow-up substantially improve functional outcome.
pitfalls: Assuming a visible perineal orifice is a normal anus without confirming its position and calibre
Attempting perineal repair or dilatation before determining whether the lesion is high or low
Overlooking the VACTERL association and missing a significant cardiac or renal anomaly
Failing to recognise a cloacal malformation and its urological implications in a female neonate
Neglecting sacral and spinal assessment, which underestimates continence risk
management: Stabilise the neonate with nasogastric decompression, intravenous fluids, and withholding of feeds while the level of the malformation is assessed
Undertake definitive reconstruction by posterior sagittal anorectoplasty, performed primarily in low lesions or in stages after a protective diverting colostomy in high lesions
Actively screen for and manage associated VACTERL anomalies with echocardiography, renal and spinal imaging, and assessment for tethered cord
Institute a postoperative anal dilatation programme to prevent anastomotic stricture
Provide long-term structured bowel management for constipation and faecal incontinence using diet, laxatives, and enema or antegrade continence regimens
Coordinate multidisciplinary follow-up across paediatric surgery, urology, nephrology, and orthopaedics with continence monitoring and psychological support
